facts.text: Mitosis is the division of a cell's nucleus that, followed by cytokinesis, produces two genetically identical daughter cells. It is used for growth, for repair, and for asexual reproduction: when you scrape your knee, skin cells around the wound divide by mitosis to replace the ones you lost. Human body cells have 46 chromosomes, and each new cell made by mitosis carries the same 46 chromosomes as the cell it came from. Mitosis works like a library opening a second branch: it photocopies every book, clips each copy to its original, then sends one of each clipped pair to each branch, so both branches get the full collection. The books match chromosomes, each clipped pair matches two sister chromatids, and the two branches match the two daughter cells.

Before mitosis begins, during interphase, the cell copies all its DNA, so each chromosome becomes two identical sister chromatids joined at the centromere. A common mistake is to think DNA is copied during mitosis itself; in fact the copying is done in interphase, and mitosis only separates the copies already made. In prophase, the first stage of mitosis, the chromosomes coil up tightly enough to see, the nuclear envelope breaks down, and spindle fibers grow out from the two poles of the cell. Spindle fibers from opposite poles attach to each chromosome at its centromere, one to each sister chromatid, so each sister is tied to a different pole. In metaphase the chromosomes line up single file across the middle of the cell.

In anaphase the sister chromatids split apart at the centromere and each is pulled to the opposite pole as the spindle fibers shorten and drag the chromatids along. Once separated, each chromatid counts as its own chromosome, so each pole ends up with one copy of every chromosome. In telophase the chromosomes uncoil and a new nuclear envelope, and so a new nucleus, forms around each set. Then cytokinesis splits the cytoplasm: in animal cells a cleavage furrow pinches the cell in two, and in plant cells a cell plate forms that becomes a new cell wall. The result is two daughter cells, each with the same chromosomes as the parent. Next in the course, meiosis halves the chromosome number to make sex cells.

If one pair of sister chromatids fails to separate in anaphase, an error called nondisjunction, both chromatids get pulled to the same pole. So one daughter cell gets an extra chromosome and the other is missing one, and the two cells are no longer identical. When the controls on the cell cycle fail, cells can keep dividing by mitosis without stopping and form a tumor, as happens in cancer.

lesson_markdown:
## How does mitosis make two identical cells?

When you scrape your knee, skin cells around the wound divide by mitosis to replace the ones you lost. Mitosis, followed by cytokinesis, turns one cell into two genetically identical daughter cells. It is used for growth, for repair and for asexual reproduction.

The big idea: **the cell copies every chromosome, then pulls the copies apart so each new cell gets a full set.**

### Think of a library

Picture a library opening a second branch. It photocopies every book, clips each copy to its original, then sends one of each clipped pair to each branch, so both branches get the full collection. In a cell, the books are chromosomes, each clipped pair is two sister chromatids, and the two branches are the two daughter cells.

### Step by step

1. **Copy every book: interphase.** Before mitosis begins, during interphase, the cell copies all its DNA. Each chromosome becomes two identical sister chromatids joined at the centromere, like a book clipped to its copy.

   A common mistake is to think DNA is copied during mitosis itself. In fact the copying is already done in interphase, and mitosis only separates the copies already made.

2. **Tie each copy to a branch: prophase.** The chromosomes coil up tightly enough to see, the nuclear envelope breaks down, and spindle fibers grow out from the two poles of the cell. Spindle fibers from opposite poles attach at the centromere, one to each sister chromatid, so each sister is tied to a different pole.

3. **Line up the pairs: metaphase.** The chromosomes line up single file across the middle of the cell.

   Each sister is tied to a different pole, so what do you think happens when the sisters let go? They split apart at the centromere, and each is pulled to the opposite pole.

4. **Send one of each pair to each branch: anaphase.** The spindle fibers shorten and drag the chromatids along. Once separated, each chromatid counts as its own chromosome, so each pole ends up with one copy of every chromosome.

5. **Open both branches: telophase and cytokinesis.** In telophase the chromosomes uncoil and a new nucleus forms around each set. Then cytokinesis splits the cytoplasm: in animal cells a cleavage furrow pinches the cell in two, and in plant cells a cell plate forms that becomes a new cell wall. The result is two daughter cells, each with the same chromosomes as the parent: in human body cells, the same 46.

### When one pair won't split

If one pair of sister chromatids fails to separate in anaphase, an error called nondisjunction, both chromatids get pulled to the same pole. So one daughter cell gets an extra chromosome, the other is missing one, and the two cells are no longer identical.

Next in the course, meiosis halves the chromosome number to make sex cells.

**Check yourself:** If a cell skipped interphase and went straight into mitosis, why couldn't both of its daughter cells get a full set of chromosomes?
